title: Viral pericarditis with effusion (low voltage + electrical alternans): enlarged globular cardiac silhouette
vignette: A 28-year-old man comes to the emergency department with a 3-day history of increasing chest tightness and intermittent sharp chest pains. He also reports mild dyspnea, especially on exertion. The patient has no prior chronic medical conditions but had an upper respiratory illness a week ago that resolved without treatment. ECG reveals sinus tachycardia and low voltage QRS complexes that vary in amplitude from beat to beat. Which of the following is the most likely chest x-ray finding in this patient?

clues.text: increasing chest tightness and intermittent sharp chest pains
clues.note: Intermittent sharp/pleuritic chest pain with tightness fits acute pericarditis, often complicated by a pericardial effusion.

clues.text: upper respiratory illness a week ago
clues.note: A recent viral URI is the classic prodrome for VIRAL pericarditis (coxsackievirus, echovirus) - the most common cause of acute pericarditis.

clues.text: low voltage QRS complexes that vary in amplitude from beat to beat
clues.note: Low voltage QRS (fluid insulates the heart) plus beat-to-beat amplitude variation (ELECTRICAL ALTERNANS from the heart swinging in fluid) indicates a PERICARDIAL EFFUSION.

whatMatters: Recent viral URI + pleuritic chest pain + ECG showing LOW VOLTAGE QRS and ELECTRICAL ALTERNANS = viral pericarditis with a PERICARDIAL EFFUSION. On chest x-ray a slowly accumulating effusion produces an ENLARGED, GLOBULAR ('water-bottle') cardiac silhouette with CLEAR lung fields. Answer A.
strategy: Read the ECG: low voltage (fluid dampens signal) + electrical alternans (heart swinging) = pericardial effusion. Then predict the x-ray: enlarged, globular silhouette with CLEAR lungs (no pulmonary edema, because pericardial pressure affects the lower-pressure right heart more). Reject hyperinflation (COPD), perihilar infiltrates/pulmonary edema (left heart failure), collapsed lung with absent markings (pneumothorax), and blunted costophrenic angle (pleural effusion).

options.text: Enlarged, globular cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields
Hyperinflated lungs with increased bronchial markings
Small, collapsed lung with absent peripheral lung markings
Blunting of the costophrenic angle with loss of the diaphragmatic contour

eliminations.label: Hyperinflated lungs - COPD
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: hyperinflation with increased bronchial markings (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: this young patient has a pericardial effusion, not obstructive lung disease. ✅ Correct if: emphysema/chronic bronchitis.

eliminations.label: Perihilar infiltrates - pulmonary edema
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: bilateral patchy perihilar (bat-wing) infiltrates of pulmonary edema. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: pericardial effusion classically leaves CLEAR lungs (it raises right-sided pressures more); pulmonary edema reflects left heart failure/acute cardiac process. ✅ Correct if: cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

eliminations.label: Collapsed lung, absent markings - pneumothorax
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a small collapsed lung with absent peripheral markings (pneumothorax). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the ECG points to a fluid-filled pericardium, not air in the pleural space. ✅ Correct if: sudden pleuritic pain with absent breath sounds and lung collapse.

eliminations.label: Costophrenic blunting - pleural effusion
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: blunted costophrenic angle/loss of diaphragmatic contour (pleural effusion). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: this describes fluid in the PLEURAL space, not the pericardial effusion indicated by low voltage and electrical alternans. ✅ Correct if: pleural (not pericardial) effusion.

reasoning: Recent viral URI + pleuritic chest pain = acute (viral) pericarditis
ECG low voltage QRS + electrical alternans = pericardial effusion
A gradually accumulating effusion enlarges the cardiac silhouette while sparing the lungs
-> enlarged, globular cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields; answer A
mechanism: Acute PERICARDITIS is most often VIRAL (coxsackievirus A/B, echovirus), classically preceded by an upper respiratory illness, and presents with pleuritic/positional chest pain. It can be complicated by a PERICARDIAL EFFUSION from fibrinous/serofibrinous inflammation. Effusion produces characteristic ECG changes: LOW VOLTAGE QRS (fluid increases the distance between the heart and the recording electrodes, dampening the signal) and ELECTRICAL ALTERNANS (beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude/axis as the heart SWINGS within the fluid-filled sac), along with sinus tachycardia. When fluid accumulates slowly (subacute), the pericardium stretches and large volumes collect, giving an ENLARGED, GLOBULAR ('water-bottle') cardiac silhouette on chest x-ray with CLEAR LUNG FIELDS - clear because the rising pericardial pressure compresses the lower-pressure right heart more than the left, so pulmonary edema does not develop. The distractors describe COPD (hyperinflation), pulmonary edema (perihilar infiltrates), pneumothorax (collapsed lung), and pleural effusion (costophrenic blunting).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid CV > pericardial effusion: causes (viral pericarditis); ECG low voltage QRS + electrical alternans; chest x-ray 'water-bottle' (globular) heart with clear lungs; risk of tamponade.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Low voltage + electrical alternans = effusion -> globular cardiac silhouette, clear lungs.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on pericardial effusion, electrical alternans, low voltage QRS, 'water-bottle' heart, or viral pericarditis? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Hyperinflation = COPD; perihilar infiltrates = pulmonary edema; collapsed lung = pneumothorax; costophrenic blunting = pleural effusion.

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.text: ECG (stem): low voltage + beat-to-beat amplitude variation = electrical alternans -> pericardial effusion; predicted chest x-ray = enlarged globular silhouette with clear lungs.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: pericardial effusion = low voltage QRS + electrical alternans; CXR = globular ('water-bottle') heart, clear lungs.

memoryHook: A heart bobbing in fluid gives faint, flickering ECG beats (low voltage + alternans) and blows up into a water-bottle shape on x-ray - lungs stay clear.
